Kenyan dairy farmers face mounting challenges as prolonged dry conditions reduce pasture, cut milk production and drive up the cost of keeping livestock [Hafsa Abdiwahab Sheikh/Al Jazeera]By Hafsa Abdiwahab SheikhPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Nairobi, Kenya – Milk is becoming harder to find in parts of Kenya as prolonged dry conditions take a toll on dairy farmers, disrupting supplies to major towns and pushing up prices.
In Nairobi, some popular brands have become increasingly difficult to find in shops. A 500ml (1-pint) packet of Tuzo, Dairy Best or Mt Kenya milk sells for 79 to 89 Kenyan shillings ($0.61 to $0.68), but supplies have been limited. New brands have appeared on supermarket shelves at about 65 shillings ($0.50) while some neighbourhood shops visited by Al Jazeera were charging as much as 100 shillings ($0.77) for the same quantity.
The shortage is being felt across the dairy supply chain, from farmers struggling to feed their animals to businesses that depend on a steady supply of fresh milk.
Farmers struggle as pastures dry up
In Kajiado County, southwest of Nairobi, dairy farmers said a prolonged dry spell has sharply reduced milk production over the past three months.
Jennifer Leshinka, a farmer in Bisil, told Al Jazeera that her daily milk production had fallen from 120 litres (32 gallons) to 50 litres (13 gallons). With natural pasture dwindling, she has had to buy hay to feed her animals. Some of her dairy animals have also been moved to neighbouring counties in search of grazing land.

Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud addresses an emergency joint session of parliament in Mogadishu [Handout/Somali Presidency]By Faisal AliPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Mogadishu, Somalia – A day before Somalia’s Supreme Court was due to rule on whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had lawfully extended his term by a year, he abruptly dismissed the chief justice presiding over the case.
On November 4, the presidency removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. Five judges proceeded with the case the following day, ruling that constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not apply retrospectively to those already in office. Their mandates, the judges said, had expired.

The government rejected the ruling and immediately swore in a replacement chief justice, setting up a direct confrontation between the president and the country’s highest court over the end of his mandate and the timing of elections.
The standoff marks the latest escalation in a two-year political contest over Mohamud’s proposed constitutional changes.
Intended to address long-standing structural problems that have hindered Somalia’s reconstruction, the changes have instead deepened divisions over the country’s political future, the nature of its federal system and the distribution of power.

A sign for Claude is displayed, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu) (AP)By John PowerPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the biggest initial public offering of all-time, leapfrogging SpaceX’s $75bn market debut in June.
The AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.
The offering represents a significant scaling up of its IPO after Anthropic said last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares and between $70 and $78 apiece.
Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT.”
The blockbuster offering gives Anthropic a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, making it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current market valuations, just behind Tesla.
Anthropic’s market debut has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the rollout of AI.

Experts say vaccine hesitancy has contributed to measles outbreaks in the US [File: Yuri Cortez/AFP]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Why the US, Mexico and Guatemala may lose their measles-free statuslist 2 of 4US loses measles-free status as two more deaths reportedlist 3 of 4US officially loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setbacklist 4 of 4US loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setbackend of list
While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.
The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.
That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.
The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.

A container is unloaded from a ship onto a truck at Tanjung Priok Port in Jakarta, Indonesia [File: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia aimed at offsetting the impact of United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The Council of the European Union’s decision on Wednesday also allows the deal to be applied provisionally. Both sides will remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products, and Indonesia’s 50 percent duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years.
The deal will tie one of the world’s top economic blocs more closely to the fourth most populous country.
“These agreements will make it easier for European businesses to trade and invest, remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia, and save businesses an estimated €600 million [$658.3m] annually in customs duties,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee.
Indonesia has been negotiating a free trade and investment agreement with the EU since 2016. However, relations became strained after the European Commission decided to phase out palm oil from transport fuel by 2030 and imposed anti-subsidy duties on Indonesia’s biodiesel exports.
Both sides want the agreement, initially concluded in September 2025, to be applied as swiftly as possible. Indonesia will graduate from the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences on January 1, 2027, after which its exports will no longer benefit from preferential tariffs, the Council said in a statement.

A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has capsized off the coast of Yenne in western Senegal, killing at least one person.
Local officials told the AFP news agency that the pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat struck a rocky area and washed ashore overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday.

An undated artist's concept shows NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft [File: Reuters via NASA]By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, the most distant human-made object, has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth nearly 50 years after it was launched.
The spacecraft hit the milestone on Wednesday and is now about 26 billion km away, according to NASA.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3SpaceX’s Starship captured by launchpad arms in dramatic firstlist 2 of 3Pakistani astronaut to join China’s next space station missionlist 3 of 3‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it mattersend of list
A light-day is the distance light can travel in 24 hours, which means messages sent from Earth take a day to reach Voyager 1, and another day for teams on the ground to receive a reply.
The feat is “the best illustration of just how vast space is”, said NASA scientist Tiffany Kataria. “So much of what we dream about is travelling to other stellar systems,” she told the AFP news agency. “And it took Voyager 1 nearly 50 years to get to just the edge of our own solar system, let alone to only a light-day.”
Many exoplanetary systems, she noted, are at least several light-years away. NASA expects Voyager 1 to take about 18,000 years to travel a full light-year.
Interstellar space
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin Voyager 2 are the only spacecraft to have reached interstellar space, the region beyond the Sun’s heliosphere. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
Some of Voyager 1’s equipment, including its cameras, has been switched off remotely to save power, but the probe continues to study invisible phenomena such as magnetic fields.
